extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) drafting and prosecuting AI/ML-related patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for preparing disclosure, claims, and specifications for AI/ML inventions and for responding to prosecution rejections. Focuses on what to disclose about data, architecture, training, inference, and how to draft claims and spec to satisfy §§101 and 112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data disclosure (pre-processing and provenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose issues encountered using collected data and how the solution addresses them; whether data is proprietary or publicly available; whether the data format changes between collection and model use; whether statistical aggregates of raw data are used; and whether input data are manipulated or transformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer disclosure questions such as: Did you encounter issues using collected data? Is the data proprietary, public, or both? Does the data format change between collection and use? Are statistical aggregates used? Are input data manipulated or transformed for use by the invention?

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-processing disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe any further modifications or processing performed on model outputs to make them usable, including whether post-processing is performed by the same or different devices/systems and the types of post-processing employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address: How is the output processed or made usable? Is there calibration or transformation of outputs (e.g., Platt scaling)? Are output data manipulated or transformed for use by the invention or downstream functions?

rubrics_metrics.name: Model architecture disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose whether the model architecture is off-the-shelf or custom, the high-level architecture used (e.g., CNN, RNN, transformer), whether multiple architectural elements are used, how elements relate to each other, and structural details of individual layers and activations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: Is the architecture off-the-shelf or custom and, if custom, how was it modified? What high-level architecture is used and how does it relate to the problem? Are multiple high-level elements used and how are they connected/arranged? What is the structure of individual layers and what activation functions are used?

rubrics_metrics.name: System integration and computing environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the broader system context in which the AI component operates (e.g., mobile phone, robot, vehicle), whether training/deployment is distributed (e.g., federated learning), sensors and control systems, user devices, databases, and other external elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer: What is the computing environment? Are there user devices, databases, or external elements? Is training or deployment distributed across components? Can an off-the-shelf model be used and why was a particular model selected (advantages)? Which hyperparameters have been set and why?

rubrics_metrics.name: Training process disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the training methodology (supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement, diffusion, autoencoders, etc.), the training data and labeling procedures, loss functions, optimization algorithms, hyperparameter settings, and how parts of the model are trained (jointly, separately, phased, frozen, pruned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address: What type of learning algorithm is used? What training data is used and how obtained/labeled (automated labeling?)? What loss function(s) are used and what components influence model performance? What optimization algorithm and hyperparameters are used? Are different parts fixed/trained separately/jointly or trained in multiple phases? Are any aspects discarded after training?

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference process disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the inference operation: what inputs are received and outputs generated, the underlying architecture enabling inference, improvements resulting from the inference, whether existing architectures are combined, and whether the trained model is updated as a result of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: What input(s) are received and what output(s) are generated? What architecture enables inference? What improvements result from the inference method? Are existing architectures combined to address a new problem or improve performance? Is the trained model updated post-inference and how? Are input data expected to change over time?

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter eligibility strategies (§101)
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting AI claims, follow the MPEP/Alice-Mayo-style evaluation: determine statutory category, whether claims recite an abstract idea, whether claims are integrated into a practical application, and whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more.' Use three basic strategies: avoid language invoking an abstract idea, include language integrating the claim into a practical application, and include additional elements integral to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid steps that sound like mental processes (predict, identify, evaluate), mathematical equations/notation, and words that invoke business/legal activities. To integrate into a practical application, include technology-related steps (e.g., improving model accuracy; reducing model size/parameters/layers; reducing training data; enabling lifelong learning; improving training speed/efficiency; increasing inference speed/efficiency; enabling/optimizing different hardware). To show 'significantly more,' include specific architectural elements, ML-specific steps (encoding/decoding, embedding, performing a convolution), steps that cannot be performed in the human mind, physical sensors or physical transformations, and non-generic hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding means-plus-function/indefiniteness (§112 risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid drafting claims with non-structural, generic terms (Module; Component; Unit; Element; Mechanism; System; Apparatus) that invite 35 U.S.C. §112(f) interpretation unless the specification provides corresponding structure. Provide more than a repeat of generic terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more specific AI terms where appropriate (machine learning model, ANN, CNN, GAN, reinforcement learning model). If non-structural terms are used, describe in the specification whether the element is hardware or implemented in software and provide sufficient structural description so the claim is not rejected as indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training-claim drafting considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that training claims can be claimable (per MPEP examples) but may be rejected; tailor training claims to avoid explicit mathematical concepts and support them in the specification as computationally intense and impractical to perform mentally. Consider novel loss functions, dedicated training architectures, and special-purpose hardware in claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe training steps in the specification with computational detail, avoid reciting explicit formulas in claims, highlight novel loss functions or training-architecture details, and consider claiming special-purpose hardware (GPU/TPU/accelerator) to overcome 'generic computer' objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference-claim drafting strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate inference claims by species: (1) standard ML model performing a novel task, (2) novel ML model performing a standard task, and (3) novel ML model performing a novel task. Tailor claim strategy accordingly: focus on the novel task, explicitly claim what makes the model novel (configurations, layer combinations), or leverage the novel task to allow broader model claiming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For (1), emphasize what the novel task is because a generic ML model is unlikely to confer eligibility. For (2), claim the specific configuration or combination of layers that makes the model novel. For (3), recite elements of the novel task to permit more flexible/broad claiming while balancing trade secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture-claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft architecture claims to recite specific AI architectural components and processing patterns (CNN, RNN, transformer, ensembles) and/or hardware aspects rather than only generic computing components. Architecture claims may focus on a portion of an architecture and be part of a complete claim set including training and inference claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference particular machine-like components (CNN, RNN, BERT, GPT) to avoid being considered generic. Claiming architectural elements shows practical application and non-conventionality. Incorporate architectural elements into method steps (e.g., 'performing a neural network convolution') and consider hardware sensors and special compute hardware as claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem/solution claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a problem, the technical solution, and the resulting improvement over prior art systems can avoid eligibility rejections even without explicit architecture or training elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure claims to identify the problem (e.g., receive a 2D image depicting an obstacle), intermediate technical solution steps (e.g., generate a depth map indicating obstacle distance), and the resulting action or improvement (e.g., navigate while avoiding obstacle using the depth map). Ensure the problem, solution, and result are fully described in the specification to support eligibility arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification drafting for §101 (use of claim terms in light of spec)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because claim terms are interpreted in light of the specification, include technical definitions and detailed descriptions in the spec for terms that might otherwise be read as abstract (predict, identify, observe, evaluate, encode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide AI/ML-specific technical definitions (e.g., 'encoding' as representing data in a high-dimensional embedding space) or describe exemplary uses of terms to differentiate from mental processes. Describe a technical problem, the technical solution, and the technology-specific benefits derived from the invention to show integration into a practical application and to support 'significantly more' arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description, enablement, and best mode (§112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the specification provides written description of the invention, describes how to make and use it (enablement), and discloses the best mode. For AI inventions, written description often maps to architecture details while enablement maps to training and inference details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe architectural, training, and inference details in virtually every AI patent application. Recognize PHOSITA uncertainty in fast-moving AI fields and provide sufficient detail so a PHOSITA could make/use the invention without undue experimentation. Disclose any preferred forms of training, architecture, and inference as the best mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness support and examples (§112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid indefiniteness, provide algorithms, descriptions of how functions are performed, what elements perform functions, how exceptions are handled, and examples demonstrating possession of the invention at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide method steps that are performed automatically (rather than relying on user actions) when possible. For well-known/off-the-shelf ML modules, claim terms may avoid invoking §112(f); for specialized ML modules, provide sufficient structural description (algorithms, inputs/outputs, exception handling). Use examples to show possession and enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three levels of description (architecture and training)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe AI inventions at three abstraction levels: (1) target function/functional component (high-level), (2) high-level technical architecture/paradigm (e.g., CNN, RNN), and (3) detailed technical description (layers, nodes, activation functions). Do the similar three-level breakdown for training: functional description, training paradigm, and fine details (loss functions, policy model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave the inventive concept into the description at each level. For architecture, relate the problem to chosen high-level architecture and provide node/layer-level details without necessarily giving actual parameter values. For training, go from 'network trained to classify' to 'supervised learning with X loss' to detailed loss components and training phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem/solution description in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: In the specification, provide a description of the technical problem in the prior art, a description of the technical solution including structure performing each claimed function (algorithms if software), and a description of how the solution yields improvements over existing systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivate the solution without conceding too much background as prior art: identify field, provide a generic device/task name, describe implementation problems, describe structure performing claimed functions (and how), provide non-limiting definitions or exemplary uses of AI-specific terms, and describe improvements that are specific and tied to the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to §101 office-action rejections (prosecution strategies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three key response strategies to §101 rejections: (1) argue the claim does not recite a judicial exception, (2) argue the claim is integrated into a practical application, and (3) argue that additional elements (or their combination) add 'significantly more' than conventional solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parallel the eligibility-avoidance strategies; implement them with AI-specific tailoring (e.g., emphasize non-abstract architectural/training elements, physical sensors, technical improvements, specific ML operations). When responding, ensure examiner has been walked through the four-step eligibility analysis and the specification supports the chosen strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common examiner rejection patterns (empirical observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical study of 200 AI patent office actions (1/1/23–9/30/23) shows prevalent rejection patterns: most rejections occur at Step 2 (abstract idea) under the mental process category, and examiners commonly view claims as using generic computer components under Step 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics: 71% rejected under mental process (42% under human activity, 15% under mathematical concept); 92% found to use generic computer components (e.g., 'computer system/product, device, memory, processor, non-transitory computer readable medium, ML model') in Step 3. Use these patterns to anticipate examiner objections and craft claims/specs accordingly.
